Churches, Cemeteries & John Paul II

St Anthony of Padua Basilica

A Polish Franciscan from this basilica is pastor to the Poles of Turkey and also looks after the parish at Adampol – and for ten years the future Pope John XXIII preached here.

Theme
Churches, Cemeteries & John Paul II
District
Beyoğlu
Period
1906–1912
Visiting
Open to visitors

The story

Amid the bustle of İstiklal, between the shops and the heritage tram, a Mass is said in Polish every Sunday – in Istanbul's largest Catholic church.

The first St Anthony's was built here by the Italian community in 1725. The present red-brick basilica, in Venetian neo-Gothic style, was built between 1906 and 1912 by the city's Levantine Italians to designs by the architect Giulio Mongeri; apartment blocks screen it from the street, and you reach it through a gateway and courtyard. For ten years Angelo Roncalli, the apostolic delegate to Turkey and later Pope John XXIII, preached here, and his statue stands in the courtyard.

For Poles it is a special church. It is home to a Polish personal parish for Poles in Turkey, run by Conventual Franciscans of the Warsaw province. Its pastor also administers the parish of Our Lady of Częstochowa in Polonezköy – the old Adampol, founded by Polish émigrés in 1842. So a church in the heart of the metropolis and a village on the Asian side of the Bosphorus share a priest, and the 19th-century exiles and today's Polish community meet at one altar. In 2021 President Andrzej Duda awarded the then pastor, Fr Michał Sabatura, the Silver Cross of Merit for his service to Poles in Turkey.

The Polish Mass is often held in the lower church; the 2024 Easter timetable lists it as 'Po Polsku (Kościół dolny)'. This, rather than any museum, is where you are most likely to meet Istanbul's living Polish community – students, mixed families, expatriate workers and visitors stepping in from the avenue to pray in their own language.

How to visit

Enter from İstiklal Caddesi (No. 171) through the gateway between the apartment blocks; the church is usually open during the day. The time of the Polish Sunday Mass has changed over the years: the Cornucopia guide gives 9.30, other sources 11.30 in the lower church – check the current time with the parish or the Polish Consulate General before you go. Please keep quiet and do not take photographs during services. Look for the statue of John XXIII in the courtyard.
